title: Purchase-to-pay walkthrough
learn: How one purchase moves from indent to payment, control by control
How to test approval, three-⁠way match and GRN timing against a policy
How to write an observation: condition, criteria, cause, consequence, action
do: Walk one purchase end to end
Test 15 purchases and follow up a bank change
Write two observations for the draft report

case.role: First-⁠year article assistant on the internal audit team
case.client: Khamang Foods Private Limited, a Ranjangaon company that makes namkeen and chikki. Its board appointed our firm as internal auditor for 2026–27.
case.team: Sameer Kulkarni (internal audit senior) and you; Ashwin Pradhan, the CFO, is the client contact
case.goal: Test whether Khamang’s purchase controls worked this year, and give Sameer two observations for the draft report.
case.where: Accounts office, Ranjangaon plant · Tuesday 17 November 2026

messages: Morning. P2P at Khamang today. Walk Shikrapur’s July box order end to end first, then test my 15 picks against their purchase policy.
The bank-⁠change log is in the pack too. Observations to me by 5, please: Ashwin wants the draft report this week.

documents.title: Purchase policy · extract
documents.letterhead:
Khamang Foods Private Limited
Plot E-14, Ranjangaon MIDC, Taluka Shirur, Pune 412220
documents.subject: Purchase policy (extract)
body: A purchase order (PO) is needed before any order is placed, except for emergency repairs below ₹10,000. Each PO is approved in the ERP as below:
A higher level may approve any PO within its own limit.
Splitting one requirement into several POs to stay within a lower approval limit is not allowed.
Three quotations for any purchase above ₹50,000, unless the item is on an approved rate contract.
Security logs every vehicle at the gate. Stores enter the GRN in the ERP within 24 hours of receipt, and QC records any rejection on it. Rejected goods go back against our debit note.

Payment only after a three-⁠way match: PO, GRN and invoice agree on quantity and rate (tolerance 2% on rate, 1% on quantity). For a service, the user department’s completion certificate takes the place of the GRN.

New vendors and any change in a vendor’s bank account need a request from Purchase, verification by Accounts (cancelled cheque or bank letter, and a call-⁠back to a known number) and CFO approval in the vendor-⁠master log.

tasks.prompt: Before any testing, Sameer wants one purchase walked from the indent to the payment: Shikrapur’s July order for 12,000 boxes. Its papers are in the walkthrough set. Put the eight steps in the order they happened.

steps.text: Packing raises an indent for 12,000 boxes; the production head approves it
Purchase gets three quotations and recommends the lowest, Shikrapur
Kavita approves the PO for ₹2,58,000 and it goes to Shikrapur
Security logs the truck at the gate with Shikrapur’s bill and challan
Stores count the boxes, QC passes them and the GRN goes into the ERP
Accounts match the bill with the PO and the GRN, then book it
The bill joins the Friday batch, which Jyoti releases and Ashwin authorises
The bank pays Shikrapur, and its account in Khamang’s books is cleared

notes.s1: Indent 0388 of 3 July, signed by the production head. The control: the people who need the boxes ask for them, and their head agrees. Evidence: the indent.
notes.s2: Comparison 0034 of 6 July: three box makers, Shikrapur lowest at ₹21.50. The policy wants three quotes above ₹50,000. Evidence: the comparison sheet.
notes.s3: PO 0455 of 8 July for ₹2,58,000, approved by Kavita that morning, inside her ₹5,00,000. The key control: approval before the order goes out.
notes.s4: Gate slip 1951, 15 July at 10:05 am. Nothing comes in without a record of what and when, and that time starts the 24 hours for the GRN.
notes.s5: GRN 1929, keyed in at 3:30 pm the same day, 12,000 accepted after QC. Khamang pays only for what stores accepted.
notes.s6: Voucher 2214 of 17 July: bill, PO and GRN agree at 12,000 boxes and ₹21.50. The key control: the three-⁠way match before the bill is booked.
notes.s7: Batch of Friday 28 August, released by Jyoti and authorised by Ashwin: two people before money leaves the bank.
notes.s8: ₹2,70,900 paid to Shikrapur’s account ending 4016, the one the vendor master held on 28 August. That is why the master itself has to be protected.

tasks.title: Follow up a bank change in the log
tasks.prompt: Shikrapur’s bank account was changed on 2 September. Read the change log, Nitin’s mail, the September payments and Shikrapur’s reminder, then answer Sameer’s three questions. Your answers go to Sameer when you move on.

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your answers on the bank change to Sameer?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Sameer. You can read your answers but not change them.

hints: Put section 5 of the purchase policy next to Shikrapur’s row in the log, then compare the address the request came from with the one in the vendor master.

questions.text: Section 5 of the purchase policy sets the steps for a bank change. Which of them did Shikrapur’s change on 2 September skip?
questions.sample: Which steps of section 5 Shikrapur’s change skipped

options.text: Proof from the vendor: a cancelled cheque or a bank letter
options.why: Nothing but a mail is on file. The log’s proof column names only the vendor’s mail, and that mail has no cheque or letter with it.

options.text: A call-⁠back to a number Khamang already had for Shikrapur
options.why: The call-⁠back column is blank. A call to the number in the master would have put the change to Shikrapur itself before a rupee moved.

options.text: CFO approval in the vendor-⁠master log
options.why: The approval column is blank. Nitin’s “Pls update in system” is a Purchase request; section 5 wants the CFO’s approval, recorded in the log.

options.text: A request from Purchase
options.why: There was one: Nitin, the Purchase Manager, raised PR-VM/027 and forwarded the mail. The request was there; the checks after it were not.

options.text: An entry in the vendor-⁠master change log
options.why: Not skipped: the change is in the log, keyed by apexec02 at 4:48 pm. The blank columns beside that entry show what was missed.

questions.text: On 26 October Shikrapur wrote that bills SCB/1187 and SCB/1203 are unpaid. What can you tell Sameer today?
questions.sample: What you can tell Sameer about the two unpaid bills

options.text: The AP executive who keyed the change has taken the ₹7,99,200; the change log and the two payments prove it.
options.why: Nothing on file shows who gained. The log shows who keyed the change; who took the money needs evidence we do not have.

options.text: ₹7,99,200 went to an account nobody verified, and Shikrapur says it is unpaid. It may be lost.
options.why: Facts first, then the risk, and no names. Shikrapur still has to confirm the account is not its own, and the bank has to trace the transfers.

options.text: Nothing yet: Jyoti has told Shikrapur that both bills were paid, so the gap must be at Shikrapur’s own bank.
options.why: Jyoti’s reply shows where the money went. It does not show the account is Shikrapur’s, and the change behind it was never verified.

options.text: Khamang must pay Shikrapur the ₹7,99,200 again in this Friday’s batch, and recover it from the bank later.
options.why: Paying again, and from whom to recover, are for Ashwin to decide once the facts are confirmed. Our job is to report what happened and the risk.

options.text: Call the mobile number given in the 2 September mail and ask Shikrapur whether the new account is really its own.
options.why: Anything in that mail came with the request. If the mail was false, you would be asking the person who sent it.

options.text: Reply to shikrapurboxes@email.com, attach the change log and ask Shikrapur to confirm its bank account in writing.
options.why: Same problem: that is the address the change came from. The vendor master has a different one, and the log would tell its sender what we know.

options.text: Tell Sameer now, with the log row, the mail and both payments, and suggest a call-⁠back on the master’s number.
options.why: A possible loss comes to me the same day, with the papers. The call-⁠back uses the number Khamang had before the change.

options.text: Ask the AP executive who keyed the change to explain, in writing, why it was made, before you tell anyone else.
options.why: Never confront anyone on your own. I take it to management, and they decide who is asked what, and when.

tasks.title: Write the observations for the draft report
tasks.prompt: Build Sameer’s two draft observations from the lines below: one on the split POs, one on Shikrapur’s bank change. Pick the right line for each part. Sameer has filled in the owners and the dates.
hints: Condition is what the papers show, with numbers; criteria are the rules broken; cause is why the system let it happen, not who to blame.

slots.label: 1 · Condition

options.text: On 4 November 2026 three POs on one indent, 0714, went to Uruli Flexipack: ₹96,000, ₹98,500 and ₹99,200. Each was within the Purchase Manager’s ₹1,00,000 limit; together, ₹2,93,700.
options.why: What the papers show, with the numbers and what makes the three POs one requirement: a single indent.

options.text: On 4 November 2026 three POs went to Uruli Flexipack: ₹96,000, ₹98,500 and ₹99,200. The Purchase Manager approved each of them above his own ₹1,00,000 limit, on his phone.
options.why: Not true: each PO is under ₹1,00,000. The breach is the split, and the shared indent shows it.

options.text: On 4 November 2026 the Purchase Manager split one laminate requirement into three POs to Uruli Flexipack so that it would skip the Head, Supply Chain, and approved all ₹2,93,700 himself.
options.why: “So that it would skip the Head, Supply Chain” guesses at a motive. A condition sticks to what the papers show.

slots.heading: Observation 1 · One laminate requirement split into three POs

options.text: Purchase policy, section 2: three quotations are needed for any purchase above ₹50,000, and yet these three POs went out with no comparison of quotations behind any of them.
options.why: Not the rule broken, and not true: all three POs cite one quotation comparison, QC/26-27/0176.

options.text: Purchase policy, section 1: one requirement may not be split to stay within a lower limit, and POs of ₹1,00,001 to ₹5,00,000 need approval by the Head, Supply Chain.
options.why: Both rules the three POs break, as the policy states them.

options.text: Purchase policy, section 1, which follows the Companies Act: every PO above ₹1,00,000 needs the approval of a head of department or of a company director.
options.why: No Act sets PO approvals. The criteria here are Khamang’s own policy and its approval table.

options.text: The ERP checks each PO against its approver’s limit on its own; it does not add up the POs raised against the same indent.
options.why: The root cause sits in the system: a check that looks at one PO at a time can be beaten by slicing.

options.text: The ERP was slow in the week before Diwali, so the Purchase Manager approved the three POs on his phone without opening the indent behind them.
options.why: Nothing on file says the ERP was slow, and approving on a phone did not create three POs.

options.text: The ERP needs one bill for each PO, so Purchase raised three POs on the same day because Uruli wanted to send three separate bills.
options.why: Backwards: the POs came first, on 4 November, and Uruli’s three bills followed them on 6 November.

options.text: Purchases of ₹2,93,700 were lost to Khamang, because the laminates were bought without the approval that the policy needs for that amount.
options.why: Overstated. The bills match the POs, so no loss is shown. What the split skipped is the review.

options.text: Purchases of ₹2,93,700 skipped the approval level the policy sets, so the Head, Supply Chain, never reviewed the vendor or the rates.
options.why: The consequence of a control gap: the decision missed the person meant to make it.

options.text: Purchases of ₹2,93,700 came in at the quoted rates, so the split did no harm to Khamang and needs no further action.
options.why: The rates being right this time does not mean the control worked. Next time the rate or the vendor may be wrong.

options.text: Khamang should make the ERP apply the limit to all POs on an indent together, and send the Head, Supply Chain, a monthly list of near-⁠limit POs by vendor.
options.why: It fixes the cause in the system and adds a monthly check that catches slicing even across two indents.

options.text: Khamang should raise the Purchase Manager’s approval limit to ₹3,00,000, so that a laminate requirement of this size never has to be split into three separate POs again.
options.why: That moves the limit to fit what happened. The limit is there so that the Head, Supply Chain, sees purchases of this size.

options.text: Khamang should give the Purchase Manager a written warning for the three POs, and ask Uruli Flexipack to put every future indent on a single PO and a single bill.
options.why: It punishes a person and pushes the fix onto the vendor. The gap is in Khamang’s own system.

slots.label: 2 · Condition

options.text: On 2 September 2026 Shikrapur’s bank account was changed on a mail from its registered address, with the call-⁠back and the CFO’s approval in the log, and ₹7,99,200 was later paid into the new bank account.
options.why: Wrong on the facts: the mail came from an address that is not in the vendor master, and the call-⁠back and approval columns are blank.

options.text: On 2 September 2026 Shikrapur’s bank account was changed by the AP executive, who then sent ₹7,99,200 of Shikrapur’s payments to an account that the executive controls.
options.why: An accusation the papers do not support. Nobody yet knows whose account it is; the bank has not traced it.

options.text: On 2 September 2026 Shikrapur’s bank account was changed on a mail from an unregistered address, with no proof, call-⁠back or CFO approval. The new account received ₹7,99,200; Shikrapur says it is unpaid.
options.why: The facts in order: how the change came in, what is missing, what was paid and what the vendor says.

slots.heading: Observation 2 · A vendor’s bank account changed on an unverified mail

options.text: Purchase policy, section 4: Accounts pay a bill only after a three-⁠way match, where the PO, the GRN and the invoice agree on quantity and rate within the set tolerances.
options.why: Nothing in the pack says those two bills failed the match; Shikrapur’s reminder treats both as genuine and due. The rule broken is the one on bank changes.

options.text: Purchase policy, section 5: a bank change needs a request from Purchase, a cancelled cheque or bank letter, a call-⁠back to a known number and CFO approval in the log.
options.why: The rule as written, every step of it, so the reader sees which steps were skipped.

options.text: Purchase policy, section 1: a PO is needed before any order is placed, except for emergency repairs below ₹10,000, and one requirement may not be split into several POs.
options.why: Not the rule in question. Nothing here turns on a missing PO; the failure is in how Shikrapur’s bank details were changed.

options.text: The ERP releases the payment batch only once a week, on Fridays, which leaves Accounts no time to check a bank change keyed in midweek.
options.why: The batch day did not cause this. A change keyed on a Wednesday could have been checked by Friday.

options.text: The ERP cannot stop a stranger outside Khamang from imitating a vendor’s mail address and then writing to Purchase in that vendor’s name.
options.why: True of any mail system, and nothing an observation can fix. The cause we can fix is inside Khamang.

options.text: The ERP lets the user who keys a bank change in the vendor master save it with the call-⁠back and CFO approval columns left blank.
options.why: Built into the system: it accepts the change on one person’s word, so the policy rests on people remembering it.

options.text: Payments of ₹7,99,200 may have reached an account Shikrapur does not own, and any vendor’s payments could be sent astray the same way.
options.why: The amount at risk now and the wider exposure the gap leaves open. “May have” until it is confirmed.

options.text: Payments of ₹7,99,200 are lost for certain, and Khamang must pay Shikrapur the full amount a second time, from its own funds, this week.
options.why: Not yet known. The bank may still trace the transfers, and whether to pay again is management’s call.

options.text: Payments of ₹7,99,200 are Shikrapur’s own problem, since Khamang paid exactly as it was told by a mail written in Shikrapur’s name.
options.why: The mail came from an address that is not in the vendor master, and nobody checked it. The control that failed is Khamang’s.

options.text: Today, ask Shikrapur to mail its bank details once more so that the master can be corrected, and release both bills, ₹7,99,200 in all, to those new details as soon as it replies.
options.why: A mail is exactly what failed. Confirm by a call to the number Khamang already had, and get the proof on paper.

options.text: Today, call Shikrapur on the vendor master’s number, stop paying the new account and have the bank trace both transfers; then make bank changes wait for a call-⁠back and approval.
options.why: Contain the loss first, then fix the system so that one person cannot change a bank account alone.

options.text: Today, stop all bank transfers to Shikrapur and pay it only by cheque until the year end, so that nothing more can go to the wrong account.
options.why: Cheques for one vendor leave the control as it is. The next false mail will be about another vendor.

That many exceptions can sound dramatic, but these were picks aimed at risk, not a random sample. Write them as control exceptions with amounts, never as fraud.

principles: One walkthrough shows the design. Testing purchases from across the period shows whether the control operated.
